formation.title: The Moroccan Sultanate
formation.text:
The lands of Morocco are united under a single throne. From the Atlas Mountains to the Atlantic coast, from the fertile plains of the Gharb to the Saharan fringe, the Sultanate commands a realm of immense strategic value.

The question that faces the new Sultan is one of vision. The path of the Commander of the Faithful calls Morocco to assert its Sharifian authority across the Maghreb and beyond, securing the frontier, conquering the Sahara, and forging a western caliphate. The path of the Gateway of Two Seas turns Morocco's gaze seaward, seizing the Strait, venturing into the Atlantic, and building a maritime empire to rival the Iberians.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

modifiers.name: The Sharif Commands the Faithful
modifiers.text: The Sultan of Morocco draws authority not merely from military power but from his descent from the Prophet. As Commander of the Faithful, his legitimacy unites tribes, scholars, and soldiers under a single banner of righteous purpose.

options.text: We are the gateway of two seas.

modifiers.name: Gateway of Two Seas
modifiers.text: Morocco commands the western Mediterranean and the Atlantic approaches to Africa. Its ports channel gold, sugar, and European goods between two oceans, making the Sultanate an indispensable link in global commerce.

advances.name: Zenata Cavalry Tradition
advances.text: The Zenata Berbers who founded the Marinid dynasty brought with them the fighting traditions of the Saharan steppe, swift horsemen who struck hard and vanished before the enemy could respond.

advances.name: Kasbah Fortifications
advances.text: The kasbahs of Morocco, fortified strongholds of rammed earth and stone, control mountain passes, guard oases, and dominate the approaches to every major settlement.

advances.name: Fez, City of Learning
advances.text: Fez has been the intellectual capital of the Maghreb since the founding of the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in 859. Its scholars preserve and transmit knowledge across the Islamic world.

advances.name: The Timekeepers of Fez
advances.text: A chamber for the muwaqqit, the astronomer who fixes the hours of prayer, was built beside the minaret of the great mosque of Fez in 1286. Astrolabes are kept in it, and since 1361 the water clock of al-Laja'i. Arithmetic and the science of the stars are taught there to those who will keep time in every town of the realm.

advances.name: Madrasa Builders of Fez
advances.text: The master builders of Fez, the maalems of carved stucco, cedarwood and cut tile, are organised craft by craft under their own wardens. The schools and libraries they raise for the sultans are copied in every town of the realm.

advances.name: Zellige Craftsmanship
advances.text: Moroccan artisans perfected the art of zellige, intricate geometric mosaic tilework cut by hand from glazed terracotta. This craft adorns every mosque, palace, and fountain in the realm.

advances.name: Funduq Trade Network
advances.text: The funduqs (merchant inns with warehouses, stables, and lodging) form the backbone of Morocco's internal trade, providing shelter and storage for the caravan routes linking the coast to the Sahara.

advances.name: Barbary Corsairs of Sale
advances.text: The corsairs of Sale and Rabat terrorize the Atlantic and Mediterranean, capturing ships and raiding coastal towns from Iceland to the Canaries. Their galleys are fast, well-armed, and crewed by fearless raiders.

advances.name: Aqueducts of the Sous
advances.text:
Aqueducts of rammed earth carry the water of the Sous for miles to turn the wheels of the sultan's sugar mills. What the wheels do not need is led on to the fields below.

Available in: Sugar Press

advances.name: Wattasid Diplomatic Craft
advances.text: Caught between Ottoman expansion from the east and Portuguese aggression from the sea, Morocco's Wattasid rulers developed a sophisticated diplomacy of playing powers against each other to preserve independence.

advances.name: Moroccan Arms Production
advances.text: The need to resist Portuguese coastal incursions spurred Morocco's metalworkers to produce firearms, cannons, and edged weapons in growing quantities, reducing dependence on foreign arms.

advances.name: Saadian Gunpowder Revolution
advances.text: The Saadian dynasty adopted Ottoman military methods (disciplined musketeer infantry, field artillery, and fortress warfare) transforming Morocco's army from a cavalry-dependent force into a gunpowder state.

advances.name: Battle of Three Kings
advances.text: The destruction of King Sebastian's Portuguese invasion at Alcacer Quibir in 1578 was Morocco's greatest military triumph, establishing the Saadian dynasty's prestige across the Islamic world and Europe alike.

event.title: The Battle of Three Kings
event.text: On August 4, 1578, the Portuguese King Sebastian led an army of twenty thousand across the Strait into Morocco, seeking to place a puppet on the Sultanate's throne. At the river of Oued al-Makhazin, near Alcacer Quibir, the Moroccan forces met them with devastating effect. When the dust settled, three kings lay dead, Sebastian of Portugal, the deposed Moroccan pretender Abu Abdallah, and the reigning Sultan Abd al-Malik who had died of illness during the battle itself. The victory was total. Portugal's army was annihilated, its king's body never recovered, and the ransom of thousands of prisoners filled Morocco's treasury. Ahmad al-Mansur, brother of the fallen Sultan, now ascends to power with the epithet 'al-Mansur', the Victorious.

options.text: Let the victory inspire our armies!

modifiers.name: Victory at Alcacer Quibir
modifiers.text: The crushing defeat of the Portuguese invasion has filled the army with fierce confidence. Morocco stands as the bulwark of Islam against Iberian aggression.

options.text: Let the world know Morocco's strength!

modifiers.name: Diplomatic Triumph of 1578
modifiers.text: The Battle of Three Kings eliminated not only an invading army but the Portuguese king himself. Morocco's reputation in the courts of Europe has reached extraordinary heights.

advances.name: Ransom of the Three Kings
advances.text: The Portuguese nobility taken alive at Alcacer Quibir was sold back family by family. The ransoms drained Lisbon of coin and filled the Sultan's mint, where Ahmad al-Mansur struck the gold dinars that earned him the name the Golden.

advances.name: Saadian Architectural Patronage
advances.text: The Saadian dynasty's patronage produced the El Badi Palace in Marrakech, 'the Incomparable', and the exquisite Saadian Tombs, monuments to dynastic power crafted from the finest materials money could buy.

advances.name: Imperial Meknes
advances.text: Moulay Ismail's transformation of Meknes into an imperial capital (with its massive walls, vast granaries, and monumental Bab Mansour gate) was the largest construction project in Moroccan history.

event.title: Moulay Ismail and the Glory of Meknes
event.text: Sultan Moulay Ismail has embarked upon the most ambitious construction program in Moroccan history. Breaking with tradition, he has chosen Meknes as his new capital, and the city is being transformed into a monument to absolute power. The massive walls stretch for kilometers, enclosing palaces, gardens, granaries capable of feeding the realm for years, and stables for twelve thousand horses. His army of Black Guard soldiers, a standing force of slave soldiers loyal only to the Sultan, numbers in the tens of thousands and enforces his will from the Rif to the Sahara. The European powers, humbled by his capture of Tangier and Larache from their garrisons, now send ambassadors bearing gifts. But Moulay Ismail's methods are as terrifying as they are effective.

options.text: Build an empire to last a thousand years.

modifiers.name: Moulay Ismail's Consolidation
modifiers.text: The Iron Sultan has imposed his will across the realm. His vast construction projects at Meknes, his reorganization of the army, and his ruthless centralization of power have forged Morocco into a formidable state.

options.text: Let our enemies tremble at our walls.

modifiers.name: Terror of the Iron Sultan
modifiers.text: Moulay Ismail's rule rests on fear and military might. His vast standing army, his network of fortifications, and his reputation for pitiless vengeance make Morocco a fortress that no invader dares approach.

advances.name: Alaouite State Centralization
advances.text: The Alaouite dynasty rebuilt the Moroccan state around a centralized Makhzen, a network of tribal alliances, military garrisons, and tax collectors that bound the periphery to the throne.

advances.name: Corsair Fleet Expansion
advances.text:
Under the Alaouites, Morocco's corsair fleet expanded from a local nuisance to a strategic instrument. European powers were forced to negotiate treaties and pay tribute to protect their shipping. The gunsmiths' streets turn to blades for the crews.

Available in: Moukahla Workshop

advances.name: The Land of the Makhzen
advances.text: The Sultan's governors, garrisons and allied tribes push the frontier of obedient country outward into the land of dissidence, one valley at a time, and the law of the Makhzen follows them.

advances.name: Early Moroccan Modernization
advances.text:
While full industrialization eluded Morocco, the late Alaouite period saw tentative steps toward modern manufacturing, including European-style workshops and improvements to port infrastructure.

Available in: Moukahla Workshop

advances.name: Moroccan Diplomatic Sovereignty
advances.text: Morocco was one of the first states to recognize the United States in 1786 and maintained sovereign diplomatic relations with major powers throughout the era, resisting full European domination longer than any other African state.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Sultanate
destiny.text: Morocco is formed and its Sultan's authority is recognized. The realm stands at a crossroads, the path chosen at formation now shapes the Sultanate's ambitions. Stabilize the realm to begin pursuing its destiny.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: Destiny of the Sultanate
event.text: The Sultanate of Morocco stands unified, its banner raised over the Atlas and the coast alike. The realm is stable, its people look to the Sultan for guidance. The path ahead is long, but the first step has been taken, Morocco's destiny is now in motion.

destiny.name: The Maghreb Secured
destiny.text: Conquer Tlemcen to end Zayyanid rivalry and build an army worthy of the Commander of the Faithful. The western Maghreb must answer to a single throne before the Sultan can look further afield.

conditions.text: Chose the Commander of the Faithful destiny
Own Tlemcen, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 30

event.title: The Maghreb Secured
event.text: Tlemcen has fallen. The ancient seat of the Zayyanid sultans, which for centuries contested Moroccan hegemony over the western Maghreb, now answers to the Sultan in Fez. With a strong army at his command, the frontier is secured and the road south to the Sahara lies open. The Commander of the Faithful has proven that his claim extends beyond Morocco's traditional borders.

options.text: The Maghreb bows to the Commander.

destiny.name: Masters of the Golden Road
destiny.text: March south across the Sahara to seize Timbuktu and the trans-Saharan gold routes. The wealth of sub-Saharan Africa must flow through Moroccan hands to fund the Sultan's ambitions.

conditions.text: Own Timbuktu, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 2000

event.title: Masters of the Golden Road
event.text: Moroccan soldiers and merchants now command the trans-Saharan routes. Timbuktu, the legendary city of gold and learning, flies the Sultan's banner. The salt caravans of Taghaza march under Moroccan escort. The wealth of sub-Saharan Africa flows northward to Marrakesh and Fez. The question is how to consolidate this vast domain, through military garrisons and punitive expeditions, or through commercial networks and settled administration.

modifiers.name: Saharan Garrison Network
modifiers.text: Military outposts along the trans-Saharan routes secure the golden road by force of arms, though the constant vigilance wears on the soldiery.

options.text: Let trade bind what conquest won.

modifiers.name: Saharan Commercial Network
modifiers.text: Merchant caravans and funduqs bind the conquered Saharan territories to the Sultanate through trade, though the far-flung realm breeds local autonomy.

destiny.name: The Western Caliphate
destiny.text: Conquer Tunis and Algiers to unite the entire Maghreb under Sharifian authority. With prestige earned through conquest and piety, proclaim a western caliphate to rival the Ottomans. Unlocks the Caliphal Library.

conditions.text: Own Tunis, or a subject owns it
Own Algiers, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Western Caliphate Proclaimed
event.text: From Tunis to Timbuktu, from Algiers to the Atlantic, the Moroccan Sultan's writ runs unchallenged. The dream of a western caliphate, a Sharifian realm to rival the Ottomans, has been realized. Scholars, soldiers, and merchants from across the Islamic world look to the Sultan as Commander of the Faithful in truth, not merely in title. The question now is how to define this caliphate's character for the ages.

modifiers.name: Caliphate of Scholars
modifiers.text: The Western Caliphate draws its strength from religious learning and cultural accommodation, welcoming diverse peoples under the banner of the Commander of the Faithful.

modifiers.name: Caliphate of the Sword
modifiers.text: The Western Caliphate is forged through military supremacy, its armies the instrument of Sharifian authority across the Maghreb and beyond. The merchants of the cities pay for the campaigns and grumble.

destiny.name: The Strait Secured
destiny.text: The Rock of Gibraltar and Algeciras are held already. Take Tarifa, from which the Castilians watch the narrows, and stabilize the realm. Control of both shores gives Morocco command over all traffic between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic.

conditions.text: Chose the Gateway of Two Seas destiny
Own Tarifa, or a subject owns it
Stability at least 25

event.title: The Strait Secured
event.text: Tarifa has fallen, and with the Rock of Gibraltar the narrows between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic are in Moroccan hands on both sides. Every ship that passes between the two seas does so under the Sultan's gaze. The corsairs of Sale rejoice, the merchants of Fez see new horizons, and the European powers must reckon with a Morocco that commands the most strategic waterway in the western world.

options.text: The passage is ours to command.

destiny.name: Atlantic Ventures
destiny.text: Develop Morocco's sugar trade into a major export industry, build up Marrakesh, where the foreign merchants come to buy it, and fill the Sultanate's treasury. The Atlantic beckons with opportunity for those who can finance the voyage.

conditions.text: The capital

children.text: Sugar is produced in the market
Sugar is traded in the market

conditions.text: Marrakesh is ours and has reached a development of 36
Gold at least 2000

event.title: Atlantic Ventures
event.text: Moroccan sugar fills the holds of ships bound for European markets. The Sultan's treasury overflows with the profits of commerce, and the foreign merchants crowding Marrakesh pay for ventures that would have seemed impossible a generation ago. Morocco has become the western anchor of global trade. The question is whether to press this advantage outward into the Atlantic or consolidate the markets already won.

modifiers.name: Atlantic Reach
modifiers.text: Moroccan explorers and merchants push into the open Atlantic, charting new waters and establishing footholds far from home, though the army's readiness suffers from the maritime focus.

modifiers.name: Market Ports of the Sultan
modifiers.text: Morocco's coastal cities become thriving commercial hubs, attracting merchants from across the known world, though rapid growth brings inflationary pressures.

destiny.name: Master of Two Oceans
destiny.text: Seize Madeira to establish an Atlantic foothold, build Mogador into the Sultan's own ocean harbour, and give it a dock for his ships. Morocco shall command both the Mediterranean passage and the open ocean. Unlocks the Dar al-Bahr.

conditions.text: Own Funchal, or a subject owns it
Mogador is ours and has reached a development of 32
Mogador is ours and a Dock, Dry Dock, Shipyard, Grand Shipyard or Naval Base stands there (Mogador must first be a town)

event.title: Master of Two Oceans
event.text: Moroccan merchants and sailors now operate from Madeira to Mogador, from the Mediterranean to the open Atlantic. Mogador has grown into a harbour that rivals any European port, the Sultanate's trade networks span two oceans, and its flag flies on waters once claimed exclusively by the Iberians. Morocco has become not merely a gateway between seas but a power that commands them both.

options.text: Our fleets shall command the waves.

modifiers.name: Oceanic Fleet of Morocco
modifiers.text: A powerful blue-water navy projects Moroccan power across both the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, establishing the Sultanate as a great maritime power.

options.text: Our trade shall bind the world.

modifiers.name: Empire of the Two Seas
modifiers.text: Morocco's diplomatic and commercial networks span two oceans, earning the Sultanate respect and influence in every court and counting house from Lisbon to Timbuktu.

units.name: Zenata Horsemen
units.text: The swift mounted warriors of the Zenata Berbers, trained in the nomadic traditions of hit-and-run warfare across the deserts and plains of the Maghreb.

units.name: Corsair Galley
units.text: A fast, maneuverable galley crewed by the fearsome corsairs of Sale and Rabat, designed for raiding merchant shipping and blockading enemy ports.

units.name: Saadian Musketeers
units.text: Disciplined musket infantry trained in the Ottoman tradition, forming the backbone of Morocco's reformed gunpowder army after the Saadian military revolution.

buildings.name: Khizana
buildings.text: An endowed library of manuscripts, kept by a warden beside the great mosque of the town. Abu Inan gave one to the Qarawiyyin in 1349, and later sultans and the brotherhoods of the south followed him. Scholars read, copy and borrow under the terms of the endowment.

buildings.name: Kasbah Fortress
buildings.text: A fortified stronghold of rammed earth and stone, controlling mountain passes and guarding the approaches to settlements. Its thick walls and strategic position make it nearly impregnable.

buildings.name: Funduq
buildings.text: A merchant inn and warehouse complex that serves as a hub for caravan trade, providing lodging for merchants, stabling for animals, and secure storage for goods.

buildings.name: Imperial Granary
buildings.text: One of Moulay Ismail's vast storage facilities, capable of provisioning an army for months. These granaries ensure the Sultanate never faces famine during siege or drought.

buildings.name: Corsair Harbor
buildings.text: A fortified harbor built to service Morocco's corsair fleet, with shipbuilding facilities, repair docks, and secure anchorage for raiding vessels.

buildings.name: Sugar Press
buildings.text: A cane-crushing mill built beside the cane fields, as in the Sous valley, with its boiling house fed by the aqueduct. Fields with a mill of their own are planted more densely, and the land yields more sugar. Morocco's sugar rivaled Mediterranean sources before the Atlantic plantations took over.

where.text: The location's raw material is Sugar

buildings.name: Zellige Kilns
buildings.text: The tile makers' yards at the edge of the medina. Squares of grey clay are fired, glazed, fired again and cut by hand with a sharpened hammer into the pieces of the mosaic.

buildings.name: Moukahla Workshop
buildings.text: A street of gunsmiths of the kind that Andalusi exiles brought to Tetouan and that the Sous copied at Taroudant. Barrel forgers, lock makers and stock carvers work side by side on the moukahla, the long Moroccan musket with its snaphaunce lock and its inlaid butt.

buildings.name: Caliphal Library
buildings.text: The library of the Commander of the Faithful, where the books of the Maghrib and al-Andalus are gathered, copied and taught. Jurists and secretaries trained among its shelves carry the authority of the Western Caliphate into the provinces.

buildings.name: Dar al-Bahr
buildings.text: The House of the Sea, a grand maritime arsenal and trading house where Morocco's oceanic fleet is built, provisioned, and dispatched to command the waters of two oceans.

list.name: The Makhzen
list.text: Originally meaning warehouse or treasury, the Makhzen took shape under the Saadis (1549-1659) and was consolidated by Moulay Ismail. The sultan's mobile court of hajib, wuzara and kuttab ruled the Bilad al-Makhzen directly while the Bilad as-Siba paid only sporadic tribute. Its instruments were Sharifian baraka, the tax-farming amins, and a corps of tributary qaids.

list.name: Jaysh Tribes
list.text: Settler-soldier confederacies granted hereditary military service in exchange for tax exemption and crown lands near Fez and Meknes. Moulay Ismail systematised the institution after 1672: 3,000 Cheraga, 4,500 Sherarda and 2,000 Udaya were stationed around Fez, while the Jaysh al-Udaya was constituted from four Banu Maqil tribes of Sus. Their loyalty was personal to the sultan.

list.name: Bashawiyya of the Qaids
list.text: Outside the Bilad al-Makhzen, the sultan governed through qaids drawn from the great tribal houses (the Glaoua of Telouet, the Mtougga, the Goundafa, the Hamadi of Ouezzane). A qaid commanded his own goum, collected the kharaj at his discretion, retained a fraction before remittance, and adjudicated alongside the qadi. The bashas of Marrakech, Fez and Meknes were senior even to the wuzara.

list.name: Karaouine and the Ulama
list.text: Founded in 859 CE by Fatima al-Fihri, the Qarawiyyin mosque-university at Fez became the senior institution of Maliki jurisprudence in the western Islamic world. Its ulema staffed the qadi courts of every Moroccan city, drafted the fatwas on which dynastic legitimacy rested, and administered the great waqf endowments. The Marinid madrasas (Bou Inania, al-Attarine, al-Sahrij) produced a literate scholar-judge class with which the Sharifian sultans had to negotiate, not command.

conditions.text: Owns Fez

list.name: Zawiya Networks
list.text: Sufi lodges built around the tomb of a wali, led by a shaykh claiming silsila from the founder. The Shadhili tradition seeded the politically consequential orders: the Jazuliyya, the Nasiriyya of Tamegroute, the Wazzaniyya, the Sharqawa of Boujad, the Darqawiyya, and the Tijaniyya at Fez from 1789. During the Maraboutic Crisis (c.1610-1660), the Dila zawiya in the Middle Atlas controlled central Morocco outright until its destruction by Moulay al-Rashid in 1668.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Diwan al-Bahr of Sale
list.text: After the 1609 Morisco expulsion drove some 10,000 Andalusi refugees onto the lower Bou Regreg, Sale-Rabat became the corsair capital of the Atlantic. From 1627 the city governed itself as the Republic of Sale, ruled by a divan of twelve to fourteen raises who annually elected a qaid and a Grand Admiral. Ten per cent of every prize funded fortifications. Moulay al-Rashid suppressed the Republic in 1668 but absorbed its admiralty as a permanent organ of Alaouite naval administration.

conditions.text: Owns Salé

list.name: Harka of the Mahalla
list.text: The Moroccan answer to the unsubduable tribe: the sultan in person, with the mahalla of harem, ministers, palace guard, jaysh cavalry and mountain artillery, marched into the Bilad as-Siba once or twice a year to extract back-taxes, punish revolt, and reinstall qaids. The institution dated from the Idrissids; Moulay Ismail and his Alaouite successors made it routine. A successful harka returned with hostages, tribute, and a renewed bay'a.
